extractions.source_title: Coffee brown-eye spot (142) - Pacific Pests, Pathogens & Weeds Fact Sheet

disease_name.evidence: Common Name Coffee spot, berry blotch, coffee brown eye spot

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Scientific Name Mycosphaerella coffeicola ; this is the name of the sexual form of the fungus; the disease is also known by the asexual form, Cercospora coffeicola .

type_of_disease.evidence: this is the name of the sexual form of the fungus; the disease is also known by the asexual form, Cercospora coffeicola

affected_parts.evidence: Small brown spots occur on the leaves, more obvious on the upper surface ... On the berries, the infections are smaller than on leaves ... In nurseries, it can cause leaf fall of seedlings and, in severe cases, stem dieback.

summary.value: Circular brown spots on leaves up to 15 mm diameter with light brown or grey centres, dark brown rings, and yellow margins; on berries, smaller irregular brown spots often on the sun-exposed side.
summary.evidence: Small brown spots occur on the leaves, more obvious on the upper surface ... The spots can grow up to 15 mm diameter; they have light brown or sometimes light grey centres, surrounded by a wide, dark brown ring, and a yellow margin ... On the berries, the infections are smaller than on leaves, less than 5 mm wide, but sometimes they cover the whole berry. Generally, they are more irregular in shape than on the leaves, brown, and mainly on the side exposed to the sun.

diagnostic_features.value: Circular spots with bright grey centres, dark brown outer ring, and yellow haloes on leaves; spore masses visible in the grey centres of leaf spots.
diagnostic_features.evidence: Circular brown spots, mostly 5-10 mm, with bright grey centres and yellow haloes, typical of brown-eye leaf spot, Cercospora coffeicola. Spores of the fungus form in the grey centres ... Look for the characteristic spots on the leaves with light brown (sometimes grey) centres, brown outside, surrounded by yellow margins.

disease_name.evidence: Common Name Thread blight, koleroga disease, black rot.

type_of_disease.evidence: White thread-like strands of the fungus, Pellicularia koleroga, on the underside of coffee leaves.

affected_parts.evidence: The fungus forms mats and threads of light-coloured growth on the underside of leaves and twigs

summary.value: The fungus forms mats and threads of light-coloured growth on the underside of leaves and twigs. Leaves appear light grey and dry at first, then blacken and fall, with dead leaves held in place by fungal threads.
summary.evidence: The fungus forms mats and threads of light-coloured growth on the underside of leaves and twigs (Photo 1). At first, the leaves appear light grey and dry. Later, the leaves blacken and fall. In severe cases the dead leaves become detached from the branches but are held in places by the threads of the fungus

diagnostic_features.value: White thread-like strands forming webs over the underside of leaves, and black threads holding detached dead leaves in place on branches.
diagnostic_features.evidence: Look for the white threads of the fungus forming webs over the underside of leaves, and causing leaf fall. Look for the black threads of the fungus that often hold the leaves in place.

look_alikes.evidence: Compare with other thread blights, e.g., white thread blight, Marasmiellus ( Marasmius ) scandens ( see Fact Sheet no. 15 ), and horse hair blight, Marasmius crinis-equi

extractions.source_title: Understanding and Managing Black Rot Disease in Coffee - Agriculture Institute

disease_name.evidence: Black rot disease is one of the most destructive fungal diseases affecting coffee plantations

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Black rot is caused by the fungus Koleroga noxia (also referred to as Corticium koleroga or Pellicularia koleroga in older literature)

type_of_disease.evidence: It is classified as a basidiomycete fungus and attacks all aerial parts of the coffee plant

affected_parts.evidence: attacks all aerial parts of the coffee plant — leaves, twigs, branches, and berries — but not the roots

summary.value: Small dark spots on leaves enlarge and turn jet black; affected leaves appear grey and limp before fully blackening. White web-like fungal threads on twigs and petioles hold dead leaves and berries in place. Young berries turn black and rot.
summary.evidence: Small dark spots form on leaf surfaces — usually near the margins or along the midrib where water tends to collect. These spots enlarge rapidly and turn jet black, giving the disease its common name. The most diagnostic symptom is dark brown or black decaying leaves, twigs, and berries. Affected leaves initially appear grey and limp before fully blackening.

diagnostic_features.value: Dead leaves do not fall freely but remain attached to branches, suspended by white web-like mycelial threads of the fungus. Sclerotia (resting bodies) visible on affected areas.
diagnostic_features.evidence: White, web-like fungal threads become visible on twigs and petioles, holding leaves and berries in place even after they die. This is a key identifying feature: dead leaves do not fall freely but remain attached to branches, suspended by the mycelial threads of the fungus. Sclerotia (resting bodies of the fungus) can also be seen scattered over affected areas.

summary.evidence: coffee leaf miner larvae leave pale yellow trails underneath the coffee leaf epidermis. The mining trails then turn into irregular brown spots on upper leaf surface. Physically bending the affected leaf will cause the epidermis to separate.

diagnostic_features.value: Pale yellow trails under the leaf epidermis that become irregular brown spots on the upper surface; bending the leaf causes the epidermis to separate. Cocooned pupae found on leaves on the lower third of the plant.

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: In Brazil, the etiological agents of phoma spot are fungi Phoma tarda (RB Stewart) H. Verm. and Phoma costarricensis Echandi, 1957 (Pleosporales: Didymellaceae).

type_of_disease.evidence: The phoma stain, Phoma spp., is a fungal disease that occurs in several countries around the world where coffee is grown

affected_parts.evidence: the fungus attacks leaves, flowers, fruits and branches of the coffee plant, producing very characteristic lesions

summary.value: Produces circular dark-colored spots of varying sizes on leaves (up to 2 cm diameter), dark depressed lesions on branches (dry shoots), and necrosis of flowers and fruits. Leaves may curve and crack at edges.
summary.evidence: On the leaves of the second and subsequent pairs of leaves, the disease produces circular spots of dark color and varying sizes, which can reach 2 cm in diameter

diagnostic_features.value: Circular dark-colored spots of varying sizes on leaves up to 2 cm in diameter; dark depressed lesions on branches that can involve the entire diameter (dry shoots); infection begins at the apical part in the terminal shoot and tender leaves; leaves curve and may present cracks when lesions reach edges.
diagnostic_features.evidence: In the affected branches, a symptom also called dry shoots (Fig. 3), dark depressed lesions are seen, which can involve the entire diameter. On the leaves of the second and subsequent pairs of leaves, the disease produces circular spots of dark color and varying sizes, which can reach 2 cm in diameter

look_alikes.evidence: When the lesions reach the edges of the leaves, they curve, may present cracks and the symptom can easily be confused with boron deficiency

pathogen_scientific_name.evidence: Coffee rust is a devasting disease caused by a rust fungus, Hemileia vastatrix .

type_of_disease.evidence: Coffee rust is a devasting disease caused by a rust fungus, Hemileia vastatrix .

affected_parts.evidence: irregular shaped spots on upper leaf surfaces. summary.value: Irregular shaped spots on upper leaf surfaces connected with yellow to orange powdery lesions on the lower leaf surfaces. Leaves may dry up and turn brown, and infected trees may prematurely drop leaves resulting in long, bare branches.
summary.evidence: The most noticeable symptoms of coffee rust are irregular shaped spots on upper leaf surfaces. They are connected with yellow to orange powdery lesions (diseased tissue) on the lower leaf surfaces where the spores are located. ... They eventually dry up and turn brown. ... Infected trees may prematurely drop infected leaves. This results in long, bare branches.

diagnostic_features.evidence: Spots mostly begin to form at the leaf edges or tips where water collects. The first lesions usually appear on the lowermost leaves. The infection slowly progresses up into the tree.
